articles.headline: Chevy Fees, Carter Konechne helping power Kimball/White Lake's postseason run
keyFacts: Juniors Chevy Fees and Carter Konechne have powered the Kimball/White Lake football team to a 7-3 record and the Class 9A semifinals.
The Wildkats advanced to the semifinals after defeating the No. 1-seeded Timber Lake 38-0 in the quarterfinals.
Kimball/White Lake will play No. 5 Bennett County in a semifinal matchup on Friday.
body: Nov. 4—KIMBALL, S.D. — For the Kimball/White Lake football team, having two dynamic playmakers in the backfield has made all the difference this season.
And with the Wildkats preparing for a semifinal matchup with Bennett County on Friday, juniors Chevy Fees and Carter Konechne have been at the center of a memorable season and playoff run.

"They're alike, but yet they're different. They're very explosive in their own ways," KWL head coach Ryan Skluzak said. "Chevy can cut on a dime and change direction quickly, but Carter's more of a make one cut and get downhill. They complement each other that way. They both can run you over and outrun you. Not many nine-man teams have the ability to have two solid options at running back. And we're fortunate that if one needs a break, the other one can step in and be ready to play."

That combination has helped fuel the Wildkats to a 7-3 record and a spot in the Class 9A semifinal round as the No. 8 seed. KWL is riding a four-game winning streak, outscoring its opponents by an average of 35 points per game during that stretch.

The quarterfinal victory was the biggest of the season, as the Wildkats knocked off No. 1-seeded Timber Lake in dominant fashion, shutting out the then-undefeated Panthers 38-0 to punch their ticket to the semifinals. Now, with a trip to the DakotaDome and a spot in the state championship game on the line, KWL will face No. 5 Bennett County at 7 p.m. Friday in Martin.

Much of the Wildkats' success has been built around the production of Fees and Konechne, who have established themselves as the team's top-two offensive threats while making big contributions defensively.

Konechne leads the Wildkats with 965 rushing yards on 127 carries, averaging 7.6 yards per carry with 15 touchdowns. Fees isn't far behind with 765 yards on 99 carries, averaging 7.73 yards per carry with 12 touchdowns. Combined, the two juniors have accounted for 27 rushing touchdowns through 10 games. Also, Fees leads the team through the air with 351 receiving yards on 22 catches and six touchdowns, while Konechne has added 161 yards on 10 receptions.
Their production has also helped KWL establish a significant advantage on the ground. The Wildkats have accumulated 2,458 rushing yards this season while allowing just 1,197 yards.

"It just gives the defense another thing to think about, and it helps give you a break, too," Konechne said. "Some of these teams only have one person that's carrying the workload, and by the fourth quarter they're exhausted. But with the way we do it, we're both fresh by the end of the game."
While the offensive numbers have been impressive, the defensive impact has been vital, too.

Konechne has been a leader on defense at linebacker, pacing the Wildkats with 71 total tackles, including 45 solo stops. He has also recorded five interceptions, returning one for a touchdown, along with two forced fumbles and a fumble recovery.

Fees has been equally important in the secondary, ranking fourth on the team with 49 total tackles, while adding an interception and two fumble recoveries. Frequently tasked with covering opposing teams' No. 1 receivers, Fees has embraced that responsibility.

"I just try to play confident and make sure I have my teammates back on defense as much as I do on offense," Fees said. "I take pride in being on the field as much as possible, so they count on me just as much as I count on them."

For Fees, his journey to becoming one of KWL's most important players began with a change of scenery. After transferring from Chamberlain as an eighth grader, he quickly found a home within the Wildkats' program and community.
"Ever since I came here, it has felt like I've been here my whole life," Fees said. "I got along with everybody here, and it's just a great community. They gave me a shot, and it's been awesome.

"We've all played with each other since seventh grade, and been pretty much the same team since then, and we all know each other like brothers," Konechne added. "It's not just me and Chevy, our entire team is special."
Skluzak has seen that connection translate into leadership, with both juniors setting an example for their teammates through their play and approach to the game.

"That junior class is pretty big, including those two, and they're very humble but yet they're good leaders," Skluzak said. "They use their voice in a positive way. They're able to engage with their teammates and keep everybody fired up. And when things go sideways, they're not ever blaming anybody."

With both players still juniors, the Wildkats have the opportunity to build on what they have accomplished this season. But their immediate focus is on the opportunity in front of them with a chance to move one step closer to a state championship appearance.
The 38-point shutout over Timber Lake has given KWL plenty of momentum, but Skluzak knows the work is far from finished.

"The win over Timber Lake is a huge program win. That's something you can build off going forward," Skluzak said. "To make a statement going up there against the No. 1 seed, and to be able to shut a high explosive offense like that out, that's just a great win for our team. But we can't be satisfied and it's time to worry about Bennett County."

articles.headline: California’s biggest election loser is Dave Regan, union boss who blew $47M on two failed ballot props
keyFacts: Labor boss Dave Regan spent tens of millions of dollars on failed California ballot measures, including a billionaire tax and Proposition 44.
Regan vowed to put another billionaire tax on the ballot in 2028 if lawmakers fail to make the ultrawealthy pay more.
SEIU International President April Verrett holds the power to suspend or expel Regan as the national union weighs misconduct charges.
body: Labor boss Dave Regan tried unsuccessfully to tax billionaires this election season, earning a humiliating, if unofficial, title: California’s biggest election loser.

Regan, who serves as president of SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, led an unprecedented effort this year to levy a one-time tax on the state’s billionaires, kicking off a nearly $400 million fight on three connected state ballot measures.

And if that shellacking wasn’t bad enough, Regan’s other pet ballot measure — Prop. 44, which could have forced community health clinics to spend 90% of their revenues on program services — was rejected by 82% of voters. The union and its political spending arm squandered $17 million on the failed measure.

“His members should be driving him out with a pitchfork,” one California Democratic strategist told The California Post. “He should be embarrassed, but he won’t be because that’s just the kind of guy who he is.”

From past failed attempts to rein in dialysis clinics to this year’s billionaire tax and Prop. 44, the strategist estimated that Regan’s union had burned through more than $100 million in members’ dues on losing ballot fights over the years.

SEIU-UHW’s committee that backed the billionaire tax reported $37.3 million in expenditures through Oct. 17. The union’s Proposition 44 committee reported another $11.1 million in expenses, and all it had to show for that effort was a 63-point drubbing.
Before results came in Tuesday night, Regan was already venting about the money billionaires had poured into what he called a “corrosive” advertising blitz.
Flanked by Silicon Valley Rep. Ro Khanna, he vowed to put another billionaire tax on the ballot in 2028 if lawmakers failed to make the ultrawealthy “pay their fair share.”

“Whatever happens tonight, the reality is … somehow lost in the flood of advertising over the last few weeks, is the reality that since the ‘One Big Beautiful Bill’ passed, 1.8 million Californians have lost their health insurance,” said Regan.

Regan and his progressive cohort argued Prop. 40 was necessary to backfill federal healthcare cuts made by President Trump. But with so much money at stake, California billionaires corralled over $330 million in combined spending across multiple committees. Google co-founder Sergey Brin personally put up more than $100 million.
Regan’s future at the union could now hang in the balance.

Politico reported that SEIU International President April Verrett has the power to suspend or expel him as the national union weighs misconduct charges and his countercharges. Regan was reelected by a wide margin earlier this year.

A law firm’s investigation corroborated several allegations that Regan threatened union officials in the fight over the wealth tax and did not substantiate his claim that rivals retaliated against him. Regan denied the accusations and said opponents of the tax were using them to undermine him.
Download The California Post App, follow us on social, and subscribe to our newsletters

There’s also a question of whether Regan and SEIU-UHW executives may have personally profited off of the effort to tax billionaires. As of mid-October, the billionaire tax committee owed the union nearly $6.3 million, including $3.6 million for canvassing and nearly $638,000 listed as campaign workers’ salaries, according to state records.
Suzanne Jimenez, chief of staff for SEIU-UHW, issued a statement to The California Post saying that a “political reckoning” is still coming for billionaires.

“Billionaire-funded propaganda may mislead voters about the consequences of these cuts today, but as hospitals reduce services, emergency rooms close and families lose access to care, the truth will become increasingly difficult to hide,” Jimenez said.

“If Sacramento fails to protect patients and deliver a real solution that makes billionaires pay their fair share, healthcare workers will pursue every available avenue, up to and including returning to the ballot in 2028 with a billionaire tax.”

A source in California’s Democratic labor movement dismissed the allegations against Regan as insider squabbling, adding that Regan’s bigger problem with voters this year was a split progressive coalition.

US Sen. Bernie Sanders and Khanna campaigned aggressively for the tax and the state Democratic Party endorsed it, but Newsom, Becerra, Planned Parenthood and the California Teachers Association opposed it.
That split “gave the billionaires a message to use beyond the losing message of ‘don’t tax us,’” the source said.
Political science professor Thad Kousser said the Prop. 40 defeat would likely be cast nationally as a “death knell for the wealth tax movement.”
However, Kousser said a federal tax would be better positioned to accomplish what Regan wanted because billionaires can move out of a state — an approach Newsom and Becerra also advocated for.

articles.headline: Discounted beer, earlier openings the hopeful solution for long lines at Williams-Brice
keyFacts: South Carolina officials announced that all gates at Williams-Brice Stadium will open two hours before kickoff to address long entry lines.
USC officials said Coors Light and Miller Lite will cost five dollars for the extra hour, alongside half-price concessions on water and soft drinks.
USC added 22 additional ticket scanners and magnetometers at key gates to help improve the stadium entrance process for remaining home games.
body: Nov. 4—COLUMBIA — South Carolina hopes it has found the solution to alleviate the long lines that have built at the gates of Williams-Brice Stadium before football games this year. It's two-fold.
Earlier openings and cheaper beer.

"We recognize that several factors contributed to delays entering Williams-Brice Stadium during the Tennessee game and we are committed to improving the entry process and overall experience for our fans," USC said in a statement. "To help accommodate the large crowd expected for Saturday's game against Texas A&M, all gates at Williams-Brice Stadium will open two hours prior to kickoff."

Before, there had only been select gates opening two hours early, with all gates being opened 30 minutes later. That and other issues have led to long lines outside the gates, which have often led to fans not being in their seats for kickoff and some claiming they couldn't get in until the first quarter was nearly over.

As for the beer? Coors Light and Miller Lite 12-ounce servings will be priced at $5 for the extra hour only (they're normally $13 for 16 ounces). For this week's kickoff, that means from 1-2 p.m. It's a bit more incentive to get into the stadium early.
There will also be 50 percent off concessions including water and soft drinks during that extra hour.

Complaints have been heard all season about the lines, particularly outside of the West stands. The ongoing construction and renovation at Williams-Brice has forced USC to re-route some of the in-person traffic and keep some gates closed, but the entrance process has also led to problems.
Fans are being asked to go into specific gates now, instead of just any gate they pick.

Then there's the ticket process. USC switched to all-digital tickets this year and posted numerous advisories that tickets would be scanned. That means, as USC said in several preseason emails and missives, that fans needed to download their tickets ahead of time and add them to their phone's digital wallets, so they wouldn't have to depend on a wireless signal on gameday to pull them up.

There is no specific number of fans that have encountered a problem with that, but the likelihood seems high as some longtime fans could have not understood the instructions or simply didn't want to take that step. So they're trying to do it at the gate and it isn't working.

Ever-popular complaints about not having enough workers to scan tickets, man the metal detectors or herd traffic have also been heard. USC has added 22 additional ticket scanners and magnetometers at key gates to help with stadium entrance.
There are only two home games left, against A&M and on Nov. 21 against No. 2 Georgia, and the stadium is expected to be bursting each time.
The Gamecocks have one chance to get it right before Georgia. Saturday is it.

articles.headline: I spent a morning with Meta VR Glasses and wish I never had to take them off
keyFacts: TechRadar reporter Lance Ulanoff tested Meta's new lightweight VR glasses during a 45-minute walkthrough.
The $1,299 device moves the heavy components into a separate puck and features 5K Micro-OLED displays with eye and hand tracking.
The Meta VR Glasses are expected to arrive next spring between April and early June.
body: Experience counts for something, and nowhere is that more evident than on the Meta VR Glasses I finally wore this morning.

These lightweight, intuitive, and engrossing VR glasses shed the weight and overdesigned fussiness of previous VR and mixed reality headsets to deliver a subtle, smart, eminently comfortable and fun wearable experience that is equally at home entertaining you with wild VR movies or expansive, productivity-enhancing virtual desktops.

Granted, my walkthrough of the $1,299 VR Glasses that are expected to arrive next spring (April-early June) of next year was a breezy 45 minutes, but that was ample time to realize that Meta VR Glasses were truly built on all the lessons of not only Meta Quest VR, but also by watching competitors like Apple and even Samsung struggle to inspire consumers with stunning but also expensive or somewhat unwieldy mixed reality experiences.

In my view, Meta's decision to move compute, storage, and battery out of the headset and into a 300g belt- or pocket-friendly puck pays design dividends. The wearable, which looks like a slightly oversized pair of sunglasses, is so comfortable that I barely felt them on my face, and after 45 minutes of continuous use, I didn't remove the 100-gram frames with a sense of relief. If anything, I was sad my all-too-brief interlude was over.

Without needing to support CPUs, GPUs, NPUs, RAM, a heavy battery, or even SD storage, Meta could focus on basic aesthetic appeal. The Meta VR Glasses feel and look spare, but in a positive way. By design, they do not cut you off from the outside world (there will be an optional light shield), so there's no need to slap a pair of animated blinking eyes on the lenses.
Granted, I had my doubts that the Meta VR Glasses would be all that immersive or inspiring, given what looked like essentially eye-sized lenses and no visible cameras, inside or out.
That all turned out to be deceiving.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Accurate tracking for an immersive experience

When I said Meta clearly learned from all that came before it, I wasn't kidding. The metaphors for setting up eye tracking were essentially the same as what I did for Apple Vision Pro (I didn't have to adjust pupillary distance, though you easily can) and, to an extent, Galaxy XR. You look at a circle of dots floating in space and, yes, use your fingers to pinch and select each one.
There are, obviously, cameras that track your eyes, hands, and the outside world. I was impressed with the accuracy, which matched what I've experienced on Vision Pro.

Equally, the first time I saw the floating menu, I was shocked at the visual quality (it's worth noting that Meta put in a pair of magnetic prescription inserts to match my eyes, and those inserts will probably add $150 to your final cost). For the record, Meta lists the Micro-OLED display resolution as 5K, and based on what I saw, I believe it.
Disney+, a TV App, Avengers: Infinity War VR experience, and a dozen other app icons floated in space, with each one puffing up as I glanced at it.

Meta VR Glasses software doesn't try to reinvent the mixed reality wheel. I had no trouble opening apps, closing them, or even moving windows around. It does add one gesture that I appreciated: scroll.

To scroll in any window, I made a gentle fist and then swiped my thumb across the side of my index finger to scroll left, right, up, and down. I was surprised at how quickly I picked this up; I think that has a lot to do with the accuracy of the eye and gesture tracking.
My experiences were limited to a handful of apps, but each one was compelling in its own way.

We started with an 8K VR Billie Eilish concert in which I was virtually seated front and center, close enough to take a selfie with the singer. The volume started a bit low for my tastes. Still, I was able to use the volume controls under the right temple to make the audio loud enough that it drowned out the voices of the Meta execs who were trying to guide me (they were watching what I viewed through a cast on a nearby PC — Meta VR Glasses can also cast to your phone).

We switched to the NBA Finals last, title-clinching Knicks game, which put me courtside. At one point, I realized the near-360 view was probably shot by a camera that was also almost on the court. Meta told me they partner with Kosmo (Hesai Kosmo), which uses relatively small 360-degree cameras to capture the action. As the game replay continued, I noticed Timothée Chalamet and Kylie Kardashian were also courtside. I waved, but they did not seem to notice me.

I played a puzzle game called Dragon Grove, which, as you might expect, featured a small, green, cartoony dragon who landed on my outstretched hand and let me pet him. I was reminded of a similar experience with Vision Pro and a butterfly. By launch, Meta expects to have 75+ hands-first games.

Meta believes that the primary use cases for Meta VR Glasses will be entertainment and productivity. On the entertainment front, I watched Avengers Infinity Wars VR Enhanced, which took the original film and then gussied it up with 360 surround VR imagery and even lets some of the characters pop out of the original film frame. It was cool but also a bit odd. Why would a director who intentionally chooses to shoot a scene a certain way want you looking anywhere else but his original film? It did, though, make the movie feel more like an amusement park ride, which may appeal to some.
Business class

On the productivity front, Meta VR Glasses basically start where everyone else spent years traveling to arrive. I had huge desktop screens all around me that I could move and resize with gestures. At one point, I placed a screen on the ceiling above me. Plus, I could take any screen and make it ultrawide. The only hiccup was when one coding screen stretched the code text into an ultra-wide, almost unreadable format. This is all pre-release software, so bugs like this are to be expected.

Like Vision Pro and Galaxy XR, Meta VR glasses have a floating keyboard, but they've also added something new to the mix: a surface keyboard. To enable it, I selected the option from the floating keyboard and then put my hands on the table surface. After a quick scan, a transparent keyboard and trackpad appeared on the tabletop. I could use them just as I would any standard physical keyboard and mouse. My only issue is that, as a terrible touch typist, the lack of any physical key response might make my typing even worse.

When I took off the frames, it felt like I'd removed a pair of glasses, not headgear doing its best with straps and head rings to lessen the load on my face. There was no afterburn on my nose or brows.

I do, of course, have questions. Like, even at the more affordable $1,299, will consumers buy into this for a big-screen experience on an airplane and when they're home alone (you won't sit next to a family member and tune out to your own VR experience, will you?). Gamers, especially those who are tired of wearing heavy headsets, will surely be interested in Meta VR Glasses, though I don't know if the Qualcomm Snapdragon Reality Elite processor (XR2 Gen 3), which can supposedly support all the apps in Quest's library, has the juice to run true AAA titles. I'm glad Meta has the productivity part worked out because I still think that may be the best play for any of these types of wearables: knowledge workers, business travelers, and enterprise.
Who knows, though, maybe Meta VR Glasses is the mixed reality headset to finally break open the consumer market. It impressed me and, to be honest, I can't wait to wear them again.

articles.headline: Pete Hegseth may take fall for Republicans’ midterm losses, despite Trump support
keyFacts: Pete Hegseth faces blame for Republican midterm losses tied to the Iran war, despite President Donald Trump defending his job performance.
Republican Representative Thomas Massie filed eight impeachment accusations against Hegseth and plans to force a House vote on his impeachment.
Democrats promised to investigate Hegseth and his handling of the Pentagon when taking leadership roles in the House next year.
body: Pete Hegseth is increasingly looking like he may take the fall for Republicans’ midterm losses, despite Donald Trump’s vocal support for his defense secretary, even calling him a champion of war.

The war in Iran, which voters and Trump have named as a key reason for Republicans’ midterm losses, “has been primarily a Department of War-led effort because you chose to take military action to resolve a foreign policy matter”, a former senior Pentagon official told CNN.

“If the president is serious about anyone taking responsibility for it, it’s Pete Hegseth,” one Republican close to the White House added in an interview with CNN. “Pete has been either dishonest or incorrect – neither of which are acceptable – about timelines, goals and objectives since the beginning.”
On Wednesday, JD Vance publicly questioned whether the Iran war was worth it and said it cost Republicans control of Congress.
Thomas Massie, a Republican congressman from Kentucky, has already filed eight impeachment accusations against Hegseth, and plans to soon force a House vote on the impeachment.
Trump has repeatedly defended Hegseth and, in speaking with reporters on Wednesday about whether he was considering replacing Hegseth, said: “No, I think he’s doing a very good job.”

Kingsley Wilson, the Pentagon press secretary, said: “The entire Department is unified behind the Secretary’s vision and will continue working to put our warfighters and America first,” in a statement to USA Today on Wednesday.

Trump has described Hegseth as a key proponent of the unpopular conflict, saying on 23 March: “Pete, I think you were the first one to speak up, and you said: ‘Let’s do it, because you can’t let them have a nuclear weapon.’”
Hegseth has been a polarizing figure in American politics and has made enemies even with his own Republican party.

Thom Tillis, the Republican US senator, told CBS News on Tuesday night that Hegseth had “a reckoning” coming and his strained relationship with lawmakers was undermining the Trump administration’s push for a $1.5tn defense spending package in Congress.

“I think after the election, we need to determine whether or not he’s the best person to bring those needs to Congress if he wants something done before the end of this Congress, which is only 60 days away,” Tillis said as the midterm results came in.

Democrats have promised to investigate Hegseth and his handling of the Pentagon, and aides say that could include everything from his handling of the Iran war to his purges of top military officers, including the chair of the joint chiefs of staff.
He could also face scrutiny over his Ukraine policy and US military strikes on alleged drug-trafficking boats in Latin American waters, which some Democrats say could amount to war crimes.

Adam Smith, the Democratic representative who is expected to lead the House armed services committee next year, promised vigorous oversight on everything from the Iran war to what he called the erosion of the “apolitical foundation of the armed forces”.

articles.headline: Malachi Toney expected to undergo surgery after injuring ankle in practice ahead of showdown with Notre Dame
keyFacts: Star Miami receiver Malachi Toney suffered an ankle injury in practice and is expected to undergo surgery, sources told CBS Sports.
Toney leads the top-ranked Hurricanes with 73 catches, 1,027 yards, and 13 touchdowns this season, making his status uncertain ahead of a game against Notre Dame.
Following the injury news, Toney's Heisman Trophy odds dropped from +290 to +800, while Notre Dame became a 6.5-point favorite.
body: The No. 1 Miami Hurricanes got some concerning injury news on Wednesday when star receiver Malachi Toney suffered an ankle injury in practice. Sources told CBS Sports' Matt Zenitz that Toney is expected to undergo surgery to fix the ankle, but there is hope within the program that the injury won't be season-ending.

Toney is the Hurricanes' biggest offensive weapon with 73 catches, 1,027 yards and 13 touchdowns this season, and his production for the nation's top team has made him one of the Heisman Trophy favorites alongside his quarterback, Darian Mensah.
Losing Toney the week of Miami's biggest game would be a disaster for the Hurricanes, as the Miami offense looks for ways to create explosive plays against a talented Notre Dame defense.
Toney's importance to the Miami offense

Last year's win over Notre Dame was Toney's breakout performance as a freshman, as he caught six passes for 82 yards and one touchdown in Miami's 27-24 victory to open the season. Toney is the top threat the Irish have to game-plan and account for with multiple defenders, and any limitations on his ability to get downfield or move in space would be a significant loss for Miami.

Toney accounts for 35.1% of Miami's receptions, 38.6% of receiving yards and 46.4% of receiving touchdowns this season. Cooper Barkate is second on the team in all of those categories with 28 catches for 372 yards and four touchdowns, and while talented, doesn't provide the same dynamic as Toney.

The Hurricanes use Toney in myriad ways, and his ability to move around formations and alignments allows Shannon Dawson to attack different soft spots of defenses and prevents easy adjustments to what Miami is doing because of their variation. If Toney isn't as dynamic (or isn't in the lineup), it allows the defense to focus more on slowing down Miami's run game.

The Hurricanes are 21st in the country in rushing offense at 202.5 yards per game and are 10th in yards per attempt at 5.49. Mark Fletcher Jr. and Javian Mallory make up one of the nation's best running back tandems, but they're made all the more effective by the respect defenses have to give to the big-play threat the passing game always presents when Toney is on the field.

Notre Dame's defense figured to face the difficult choice of sending more bodies into the box to slow the run or keep help over the top to prevent Toney from getting loose. The ripple effects extend well beyond the Hurricanes' passing game.
Heisman Trophy implications

Beyond the impact Toney's injury will have on Miami's biggest game of the season, Saturday's game against Notre Dame figured to be Toney (and Mensah's) best opportunity to author a Heisman moment on a big national stage.

Toney was second in the Heisman Trophy odds coming into the week at +290 at FanDuel Sportsbook -- only trailing Mensah at +170. After the injury news was reported on Wednesday, Toney dropped all the way to +800, which is now fourth on the odds sheet. Toney's injury could also impact Darian Mensah's Heisman chances, as his passing productivity would likely take a hit if his best receiver can't play or is limited.

As a result, Ohio State receiver Jeremiah Smith is back to the top spot in the odds at +170, Mensah has slipped a touch to +200, and Notre Dame quarterback CJ Carr jumps to +700 as the Irish have moved out to a 6.5-point favorite over the Hurricanes.
CBS Sports will continue to provide updates on Toney's status as the week progresses and more information becomes available.

articles.headline: GOP braces for mad dash to push conservative bills through Congress before Dem takeover
keyFacts: Congressional Republicans are rushing to advance conservative legislation and confirm President Trump's nominees before Democrats take control in January.
Priorities include preventing a December 11 government shutdown, passing a defense spending package, and confirming judicial appointments.
The House is set to reconvene next week as Republican leaders face attendance struggles, internal divisions, and upcoming leadership elections.
body: WASHINGTON — Now that the clock is ticking on the GOP’s slim majority in Congress, Republicans are scrambling to push through as much of their conservative agenda as possible before Democrats storm to power in January.

Top of the agenda will be preventing the Dec. 11 government shutdown, attempting to pass the so-called “reconciliation 3.0” package to plus up the Pentagon’s budget, and confirming President Trump’s nominees.

But Republican leadership will be grappling with an unruly House majority that has deadlocked on agenda items this year and likely struggles with attendance due to the blow to morale from the midterms.
“[Senate Majority Leader John] Thune, everybody else, it’s time to wake up and smell the coffee,” Trump adviser Jason Miller told “The War Room” podcast Wednesday.
“You have one job. Get everything on President Trump’s agenda through in the limited days we have. Otherwise, your careers are in the crosshairs.”

Republicans were dealt a historic bloodbath in the midterms, with Democrats poised to claim one of their largest House majorities in almost two decades and a massive Senate majority that could see the GOP locked out of power in the upper chamber until the 2030s.
That means Democrats will be able to stall Trump’s picks for the judiciary during his final two years in office and could hamper conservative judicial appointments into the next decade.

“I’m keeping my nose to the grindstone and will continue working through the end of this Congress to confirm President Trump’s highly qualified, constitutionalist judges,” Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) has said about his plans.
The House is set to reconvene next week.

Before lawmakers broke for recess prior to the midterms, Republicans had been teeing up a “reconciliation 3.0” package, which includes an array of outstanding agenda items, including roughly $60 billion for defense spending, and a watered-down version of the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) Act.
The SAVE Act would require proof of citizenship to vote.

Republicans sought to leverage the Senate reconciliation process, which bypasses a 60-vote filibuster from Democrats to wrangle their agenda through. But they had been dogged by differences over what the bill would entail.
When lawmakers return to session, Republicans will also have a reckoning over their leadership, now that House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) has announced he won’t seek to become minority leader.
House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) and House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) have all thrown their hat in the ring to become the top Republican honcho in the lower chamber.

articles.headline: Democrats won Congress. But can they deliver on their promises?
keyFacts: Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the United States midterm elections.
Democrats plan to use congressional committees and oversight powers to investigate the Trump administration and companies.
President Donald Trump has threatened to veto Democratic legislation, limiting what the party can accomplish without Republican support.
body: Democrats rode a blue wave to victory in the United States midterm elections, winning control of both chambers of Congress. Now comes the question of whether they can deliver on their promises.
The party campaigned on bringing down the cost of living, ending the war on Iran and holding President Donald Trump accountable, as well as pushing back against his immigration crackdown.
But Democrats won’t take control of Congress until January. Even then, there’s only so much they’ll be able to do without Republican cooperation.

Most bills need 60 votes to get past a filibuster in the Senate, and even if Democrats manage that, Trump can still veto their legislation. He has already threatened to do just that, telling a podcast on Monday, “I’ll veto everything.”
But the Democrats now also have other tools at their disposal, including power over Senate confirmations and control over committees that can launch investigations.
So what can Democrats realistically accomplish over the next two years, and where might they struggle to make good on their promises?
Can Democrats bring down the cost of living?

Affordability was one of the biggest issues for voters heading into Tuesday’s midterm elections, and Democrats seized on that, promising to bring down the costs of energy, housing, healthcare and groceries.

Dean Baker, an economist and cofounder of the Center for Economic and Policy Research, a US-based think tank, said one of the most effective things Democrats can do to bring down costs is push for an end to the war on Iran.
Since February, the conflict has driven up energy prices, as Iran has restricted commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for the oil and gas trade.
Baker argued that Democrats could use congressional investigations and oversight to pressure the Trump administration to end the war, potentially helping to give consumers relief.
Foreign policy is an area where some Republicans could find common cause with Democrats, said Baker.
Another area, he added, might be healthcare, an issue that similarly hits voters in the pocketbook.
The expiration of enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies in 2025 has left many Americans facing higher insurance premiums.
With their new congressional majorities, Democrats could push to restore those subsidies and reverse cuts to Medicaid, the government healthcare programme for low-income Americans.

A possible path to accomplishing that goal would be to include those measures in government spending bills that Congress needs to pass, according to Baker. That would also make them harder for Trump to reject.

“Republicans living in a post-Trump world, I don’t think they want to be on the side of preventing people from getting healthcare or basically paying more for healthcare,” Baker said. “They can make the politics such that he doesn’t want to veto it.”

Trump’s tariff campaign is another factor driving up consumer costs. But Baker warned that they could be tougher to reverse, without substantial support from Republicans to override a Trump veto. Even if they do manage that, prices could take a while to actually drop.

“Prices are like rockets and feathers. They shoot up like rockets; they come down like feathers,” said Alex Jacquez, chief of policy and advocacy at Groundwork Collaborative, a progressive economic think tank.
Jacquez, however, pointed to another path Democrats could take that wouldn’t need Trump’s approval.
With majorities in Congress, Democrats could wield congressional committees to investigate companies that have been raising the prices of everything from groceries to electricity bills.
“There’s a lot of precedent for getting some real material outcomes just through having the gavels and being able to subpoena CEOs and haul people in front of Congress,” Jacquez told Al Jazeera.
While there’s no guarantee these investigations would bring down prices, they could put pressure on companies to explain or adjust their decisions.
Could a Democratic Congress hold Trump accountable?
Laura Blessing, a senior fellow at Georgetown University’s Government Affairs Institute, expects Democrats to make extensive use of their new investigative powers.
“In terms of time spent and newspaper ink spilled, this is where you’re going to see the most action from Dems, by a mile,” she told Al Jazeera in an email.
Congressional investigations do not require White House approval. But they could make life harder for Trump by scrutinising his actions both within and outside of government.
Many Democrats have signalled they plan to investigate the source of the Trump family’s wealth as part of January’s incoming Congress.
Trump’s personal wealth has soared by about $2.2bn since the start of his term, according to financial disclosure forms released earlier this year.

His family’s business empire has likewise expanded over the last two years into everything from cryptocurrency and drones to artificial intelligence and prediction markets — industries his government has favoured in its policies.
Democratic senators have already been laying the groundwork for potential investigations, sending letters to companies and government departments demanding that they preserve records.

Among the issues they could examine are whether donors to Trump’s White House ballroom received favourable treatment from the government, and whether the Justice Department targeted his political opponents.
There is no guarantee, however, that everyone will cooperate.

Trump administration officials could challenge subpoenas in court, delaying investigations. But while Blessing doesn’t expect “Trump’s nuclear family to show up to a subpoena”, she said Democrats could still question government employees and others connected to Trump’s inner circle.
Even if they uncover wrongdoing, however, there is no guarantee of legal consequences, since it’s Trump’s own Justice Department that would have to decide whether to take up the cases.

Impeachment is another possibility. Lawmakers have already introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for multiple reasons, including allegations that he waged war against Iran without seeking congressional approval first.
Republican Representative Thomas Massie has said he will try to force a House vote on Hegseth’s impeachment when the outgoing Congress returns to session next week.

Trump, who was impeached twice during his first term, however, dismissed the prospect of facing a third impeachment himself, telling reporters on Wednesday that he was “not even a little bit” worried.
“I think it would destroy the Democratic Party if they did that, because it would be impeachment for no reason,” he said.
Trump also defended Hegseth, saying he was doing “a very good job”.
Even if the House of Representatives votes to impeach a government official, the case must still be weighed in a Senate trial.

Removing an elected official would require a two-thirds vote in the Senate, meaning many Republicans would need to get on board to oust a figure like Trump or Hegseth. No president in US history has ever been removed from office as a result of an impeachment proceeding.
Could Democrats end the war on Iran?

With less than two months until the 120th Congress is sworn in, experts anticipate Trump will use his final weeks with the outgoing Republican majorities to push through any remaining legislative priorities.

It also leaves Trump a critical window in which to escalate the war on Iran, according to Trita Parsi, the executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, a foreign policy think tank.
“He has shown a pattern in which, in the face of humiliation and defeat, he becomes more reckless,” Parsi told Al Jazeera.

Democrats could pursue a binding resolution to wind down the war. After all, the US Constitution assigns Congress the sole authority to declare war, and laws like the War Powers Act of 1973 give lawmakers a path to ending unauthorised conflicts past the 60-day mark.
But there is no guarantee that those efforts would work, given the possibility of Trump vetoing their proposed measures.
Experts, however, say there is another way that Democrats could rein in Trump’s war powers. One of their most powerful tools will be control over government spending.
The Trump administration can continue using money already allocated for military operations, but Democrats could try to block additional funding for the war.
“It creates a limitation for how long he can pursue the war,” Parsi said. “If he needs more funding for it, we’re not talking about small sums that he can just reallocate from other places easily.”
With control of congressional committees, Democrats could also investigate the administration’s conduct during the war, including whether its military operations complied with US law.

“Rigorous oversight would not restrict military operations by itself but could raise the political costs of the war beyond what the president or other key officials are willing to endure,” said David Janovsky, a policy analyst at the Project on Government Oversight.
How much political will Democrats have to end the conflict, however, is an open question.
Blessing, the government affairs fellow, noted that the party has historically been reluctant to withhold military funding out of fear of being accused of undermining US troops.
But Parsi warned that failing to act would be politically unsustainable — and could be seen by the party’s base as a tacit endorsement of US military involvement in the Middle East.
“It will no longer be just Trump’s war,” Parsi said. “They will also co-own it, because they will be complicit, because they have the ability to stop it.”
Could Democrats rein in Trump’s immigration crackdown?
Another target for the incoming Democrat-led Congress could be Trump’s hardline immigration crackdown.

His pledge to oversee the largest mass deportation in US history has sparked widespread public backlash. A public opinion poll earlier this year found that 65 percent of Americans believe Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has “gone too far” in its efforts.
With control of both chambers of Congress, Democrats could launch investigations into ICE and other agencies involved in the crackdown.

Their probes could seek information about conditions inside detention centres, allegations of abuse and how taxpayer dollars are being used for immigration enforcement, said Heidi Altman, the vice president of policy at the National Immigration Law Center.
Altman argues Congress could also claw back the roughly $240bn already given to the Trump administration for immigration enforcement over the past two years.
That amount of money, she explained, has allowed ICE to operate with few constraints, without having to prioritise which communities to go into or who to detain.

“The only way to force a slowdown and actual sort of decision-making and prioritisation and enforcement is to dramatically curtail their budget by taking back the funding from the last session,” she said.
Doing so would require passing legislation that Trump could eventually veto. But Altman argued that Democrats should push ahead anyway.
“The worst possible thing we could do is throw up our hands and say we have limited power,” she said.
“Pass the bills, see what happens, put them on the president’s desk, and dare him to look at the American people and say he’s not signing something that they overwhelmingly demanded.”

articles.headline: X says its updated web app is way faster
keyFacts: X is rolling out an updated web app for signed-in users one country at a time.
Principal engineer Yagiz Nizipli said the new app loads profiles much faster over slow connections.
The updated web app is already active for logged-out users and search engine crawlers.
body: X is introducing a new version of its web app that it says is much faster than before, and it’s now rolling out the updated app “one country at a time” for signed-in users.
X says its updated web app is way faster
X is moving signed-in users to its new web app one country at a time, but it’s already using the rewrite for X’s logged-out web experience.

“Open a profile on X.com over a slow connection,” principal engineer Yagiz Nizipli said in a blog post about the changes. “On the old web app, you’d stare at the X logo for more than 22 seconds before the first post appeared. On the new one, it shows up in 2.7.” The post also goes into technical detail about how the updated app “replaces the three servers we used to run for people, search crawlers, and link previews with one.”
Security researcher Jane Manchun Wong posted that she had access to the updated app, and said it “feels snappy, loads fast and many parts are polished.”
The new app is already available for the logged-out version of X.com and for the pages that are crawled by search engines, Nizipli said.

articles.headline: Trump pressures Senate on Sunshine Protection Act over ‘ridiculous’ early sunsets
keyFacts: President Donald Trump urged the Senate to pass the Sunshine Protection Act to make daylight saving time permanent and avoid early sunsets.
Sen. Tom Cotton has blocked the legislation, citing safety concerns for children walking to school and commuters during delayed winter sunrises.
The fate of the bill remains uncertain as the Senate faces a limited number of scheduled legislative days before a new Congress is sworn in.
body: President Donald Trump on Wednesday pushed the Senate to pass the Sunshine Protection Act, expressing frustration over what he called “ridiculous” early sunsets.

The Sunshine Protection Act, which would make daylight saving time permanent nationwide, has already passed the House but is still awaiting Senate approval. Trump said he was waiting to air out his grievances over the bill’s standstill until after the election , which saw Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress.

“Too bad the Senate has not yet approved the Sunshine Protection Act or, the I Don’t Want to Change My Clocks Anymore Act,” Trump said in a Truth Social post . “It’s so dark outside, so early (Sunset was 5:06 P.M., and it was dark by 5:31 P.M. — Isn’t that ridiculous?). Just a few days ago it was so nice and sunny at this same time.

“In addition, everyone’s been running around changing their clocks all over the place,” he wrote. “I didn’t want to make a big deal out of this prior to the Election because I didn’t want to have certain Senators lose their Race, in a landslide, but it is too bad they can’t get it done. The House sent it over to the Senate with great bipartisan support, numerous times (308-117), but the Senate didn’t take it up. We have far bigger priorities, but I will keep fighting for this!”

Sen. Tom Cotton (R-AR), who secured reelection Tuesday night, has been a major roadblock for the bill, which passed the House in July. Cotton has opposed ending daylight saving for years, arguing that children would head to school before sunrise and commuters could face safety risks during the winter months. Permanent daylight saving time would provide later sunsets during the winter, but it would also substantially delay sunrise.

Trump has previously blamed Cotton for the bills stalling and had claimed his opposition was “for reasons unknown.” He had hoped for the legislation to hit his desk before Nov. 1, when clocks fall back. At one point, Trump’s frustration boiled over and he released Cotton’s personal cellphone number.
TRUMP RELEASES TOM COTTOM’S CELLPHONE NUMBER OF DAYLIGHT SAVING TIME BILL

The debate over daylight saving time is not new. Nearly every state has weighed legislation related to daylight saving time in the past decade. Due to federal law, states cannot end daylight saving time without congressional approval.
The fate of the Sunshine Protection Act is unknown following Democrats securing the majority in the Senate. The lame-duck Senate has 22 legislative days scheduled before the new Congress is sworn in.

articles.headline: The Elder Scrolls 6 is reportedly more than two years away, and some fans are not coping well
keyFacts: Bethesda announced the title of The Elder Scrolls 6 as Sentinel and warned that the game is still a long way off.
Reporter Jason Schreier stated that the game is more than two years away, which sparked mixed reactions and fan theories on Reddit.
Fans responded with skepticism, various release date theories, and speculation about the game's marketing.
body: Yesterday, after eight years of waiting, Bethesda finally gave The Elder Scrolls 6 a title: Sentinel. It then warned that, after eight years of waiting, more waiting is in store because "it'll be some time before we're ready to share more." Then Bloomberg's Jason Schreier, one of the industry's best-known and most reliable reporters, weighed in, saying the game is "still more than two years away."
You know what comes next, right?

Schreier's 'two more years' statement, echoed by Jez Corden of Windows Central, attracted quite a range of comments, not all of them of the polite sort. That led Schreier to Reddit, where he could elaborate on his statement.

Pointing out his record of accurate calls on previous Bethesda releases Fallout 76 and Starfield, Schreier wrote, "I'm a reporter. I am not telling you this because I enjoy watching people get mad about having to wait for sequels to their favorite video games. I am telling you this because it is true, and because my job is to report accurate facts and clear up misinformation. TES6: Sentinel is more than two years away."
Did this clarification calm the roiling waters? Well...

Many of the replies are understanding, grateful, and sympathetic to Schreier's plight, but there are plenty that express doubt or distrust, suggesting that the two year window was pure speculation. Others want to know why Bethesda would drop the title announcement yesterday if the game really is that far out, given that Todd Howard has previously expressed regret about revealing The Elder Scrolls 6 so prematurely in the first place. Why repeat that mistake?
A few optimistic souls are holding onto the dream of a 2027 release that emerged from the reveal trailer for Skyrim on the Nintendo Switch 2:
Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

And then there are the Elder Scrolls fans operating on a whole different level from the rest of us. Redditor Reacryoum, for instance, thinks Bethesda is leading up to a surprise trailer drop on November 11—that's actually one of the more grounded theories to emerge over the past 24 hours. Casting back to one of Bethesda's old Twitter posts, Jayehemcee speculated that the theme of the game is "time," and that this is all part of the game's marketing. I'm not sure how that one works in practice, frankly, but I respect the ambition.

Minimum-Act-7571 put forth the idea that Bethesda is actually messing with Schreier by intentionally feeding him false information, because it's super mad at him spilling the beans all the time—although they also admitted that it's a "new copium theory," and so perhaps not meant to be taken entirely seriously.
I think the best of the bunch, though, is this one from Any-West7160, who believes the Sentinel title reveal contains the actual release date: November 11, 2027. I don't believe it, but I like it.
Here's the video in question—what do you see in the stars?

The best videogame conspiracy theories are always the most bonkers, but what complicates the situation just a wee little bit for Sentinel is that one such theory was actually correct: The Sentinel subtitle was stashed away in a Starfield easter egg for years before anyone noticed. Maybe it was just a coincidence, sure, but the numbers don't lie, as the saying goes—and those numbers said Sentinel. And they were right!

So there's precedent there, pretty certainly, but it's also a lot easier to drop in a reference to a locked-in-stone game title than it is to do the same with a relatively far-off launch date that's subject to disruption and delays. And as others have pointed out, including Schreier, it's extremely unlikely that anyone is just lying about the far-off release window for a little bit of PR pop: Evasion and word games are one thing, but straight-up dishonesty will leave your credibility in shreds pretty much instantly.

What it all adds up to, ultimately, is this: Two more years of waiting and maybe more, plenty of hopium and copium along the way, and a wise piece of advice from Vanquisher_84 which will almost certainly go unheeded:
See you in 2029?

From there he graduated to the glory days of Sierra Online adventures and Microprose sims, ran a local BBS, learned how to build PCs, and developed a longstanding love of RPGs, immersive sims, and shooters. He began writing videogame news in 2007 for The Escapist and somehow managed to avoid getting fired until 2014, when he joined the storied ranks of PC Gamer. He covers all aspects of the industry, from new game announcements and patch notes to legal disputes, Twitch beefs, esports, and Henry Cavill. Lots of Henry Cavill.

articles.headline: Data Center Backers Suffer Near-Total Midterm Defeats Across the Country
keyFacts: Voters passed approximately 40 measures restricting new data center construction during the 2026 midterm elections, according to the article.
Polls by Pew Research and other groups indicate that Americans oppose data centers due to concerns about electricity bills, water usage, and environmental impacts.
Democratic control of Congress and shifting public opinion could lead to increased scrutiny, delayed projects, and reduced tax breaks for data centers.
body: The 2026 midterm election blue wave, which shifted the balance of power in Congress and across state races toward Democrats, can be seen as a repudiation of AI and the controversial data centers that provide its computing power. Data center proponents have heavily backed President Donald Trump and Republican candidates, underscored by xAI CEO Elon Musk investing hundreds of millions of dollars into Texas midterm campaigns to support the industry.

But in many parts of the country, voters didn’t need to make their voices on data centers heard through candidates. They had direct initiatives on the ballot this week that would decide whether data center projects would move ahead in their districts.

In line with a growing backlash against data centers and AI, voters supported about 40 election-day measures that would restrict the construction of new data centers, with only one result — in Harwood, North Dakota — favoring data center expansion.
More from CNET
(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)
As broken down by the website Data Centers on the Ballot, Ohio had the most number of voting measures: 21, all of which were in favor of restrictions.
Maine, Illinois, Kansas, New Jersey, California, Florida, Nevada, North Dakota and Wisconsin were the other states with data center voting.

Six elections were held earlier in 2026 in California, Michigan, New Hampshire and Wisconsin, with all of them finding voters opposed to allowing data center builds to continue without new restrictions.

Not all the proposed restrictions were the same. In some elections, voters decided whether to impose a megawatt cap on data center energy use, while other measures addressed specific zoning issues or whether data center projects should require voter approval. Some proposed an outright ban on new data centers, and six of those were successful.

Polls by groups including Pew Research have found Americans have soured on data centers due to high electricity bills, water use and environmental concerns, among other reasons. It’s also hard to separate concerns about data centers from concerns about AI affecting jobs. AI has also become a divisive enough issue to affect midterm voting.
More bad news for data centers and their supporters

The election results were so bad for the industry that Politico declared data centers to be “the midterms’ other big loser” next to Republicans. Not only did voters enact additional restrictions on builds across the country, but data centers were mentioned in Democratic victory speeches.
“I do not work for data centers. I do not work for Wall Street. I work for you, I work for Ohio,” Senator-elect Sherrod Brown said in his victory speech Tuesday night.
USA Today reported that two mayors, one in Oklahoma and one in Ohio, were recalled after public backlash over proposed data centers.
What’s next for data centers
The midterms might have longer-term effects for tech companies and data center firms. It’s likely that with Democratic control of Congress, there’ll be more scrutiny.

“Public policy is going to reflect public opinion, and there’s been a very substantial change in public opinion just over the last year,” Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, told Politico.

Political headwinds from the midterms could lead local officials across the country to gain public favor by delaying or canceling data center projects or putting pressure on the companies behind them to offer more attractive deals to communities. The days of huge tax breaks and incentives for data centers could be coming to a close.

“Now, (communities) are pushing data centers to pay taxes, create their own power plants, pay for their use of electricity and water and contribute to local community resources like education funds,” The New York Times reported.

articles.headline: Building AI factories at enterprise scale
keyFacts: IDC reports that the worldwide server market grew 30 percent in a single year to reach $122.6bn in early 2025.
ASUS announced a full-stack Enterprise Agentic AI Solution at the GTC show in Berlin to help enterprises build in-house AI infrastructure.
ASUS executives stated that agentic AI workloads create heavy CPU dependency and hardware bottlenecks that require specialized cooling and server designs.
body: AI has become a juggernaut, driving technical strategy in the tech sector and outside of it. With the worldwide server market growing 30 percent in a single year to hit $122.6bn in the first quarter of 2025, IDC now feels safe recategorizing AI-driven investment "from cyclical to durable".
The analyst company expects inference to account for over 70 percent of computing demand by next year, adding that it's growing fastest at the edge.
Why enterprises are building their own

All this investment in AI infrastructure might once have come mainly for hyperscalers, but that's changing quickly. Adoption is spreading quickly beyond public cloud service providers into enterprise environments, IDC adds. They're eager to run agentic AI in-house.

There are plenty of reasons for companies to own their own AI infrastructure rather than offloading it to the cloud. One of these is data control, especially in regulated sectors such as finance, healthcare, manufacturing, and the public sector that have sovereign data requirements. Another revolves around the need for predictable costing from tokens delivered on tunable in-house systems.

So what should companies look for in a supplier? Delivery speed will be a powerful driver for many who are under the gun to deliver AI initiatives for the business, especially during periods of constrained memory and CPU supply. Life cycle services will also come near the top of the list, for companies that need help managing everything from the power through to the reasoning LLM models and the workloads that use them. That need for expertise is unlikely to stop; companies will undergo changes in AI strategy as they get to grips with a still-evolving technology.
From the desk to the datacenter

ASUS expects this AI surge to continue in the datacenter, but elsewhere too, specifically in edge locations (especially industrial use cases) and at developers' desks, as the applications that will power the enterprise get made. It wants to be top of peoples' list for hardware and services at all these places along the AI continuum.
At NVIDIA's GTC show in Berlin on Oct 21-22, it announced a full-stack AI offering that it's calling its Enterprise Agentic AI Solution . It's three-layer affair, featuring:
ASUS AI Server and Infrastructure: Its selection of AI servers, including several new units.
ASUS AI Software Stack: Its software for integrating and controlling AI workflows.
ASUS AI HUB: A services operation that ties it all together.

These bring together some existing assets that ASUS had for enterprise AI users, along with some new ones. The time is right for an end-to-end offering with new hardware because of the way the market is shifting, say ASUS execs.

"ASUS servers help enterprises build high-performance agentic AI infrastructure capable of supporting both complex task execution and large-scale AI agent deployment, accelerating enterprise adoption of agentic AI," says Paul Ju, senior vice president and head of infrastructure solution BG at ASUS.
While generative AI initially spiked demand, the advent of agentic AI has sent compute demand into overdrive. Ju explains that the focus is expanding from the GPU.

"Historically, AI servers have been optimized primarily around GPU compute. But as enterprise AI shifts toward agentic AI, workloads increasingly revolve around a continuous ‘agent loop’ that is heavily CPU-dependent," he says. That loop takes in task planning, code execution, external tool invocation, and reflection or correction work.
The CPU's increased role in this execution work is creating bottlenecks in conventional AI servers, he adds.

The first such sticking point is single-thread performance, which leaves GPUs idling while they wait for CPUs to complete. The second lies in memory bandwidth. When this is managed on a per-core basis, it can slow things down when many agents run at once.

The multi-die design of many CPUs also penalizes them in AI environments, because accessing data across dies introduces latency, Ju argues. CPUs with cores and cache on different dies suffer latency when data has to cross between them. Maintaining cache coherency exacerbates that problem.
Finally, there's a security risk: a lack of hardware level sandbox isolation on some CPUs make it possible for prompt injection to reach core systems, he warns.

Customers also bring their own challenges as they grapple with different applications for AI. Enterprises evaluating AI server options have to match their server platforms to the projected AI workload profiles, Ju adds. Training a supervised learning model to batch-classify insurance claims takes different technical resources to running a low-latency reasoning employee chatbot.
What ASUS took to Berlin
ASUS wants to help customers solve problems like these wherever they come up. With this in mind, the company had plenty of goodies for onlookers at GTC.

Starting at the datacenter, the company announced both single and full-rack systems built around the NVIDIA HGX Rubin NVL8 eight-GPU server board. It has a 3U hybrid-cooled system, the XA NR11-E12L, along with the 2U 100 percent liquid-cooled XA NR11-E12, both targeting large AI reasoning workloads.

The two Rubin units target different use cases. The 3U hybrid liquid cooling system uses direct-to-chip liquid cooling on the 8GPU baseboard, along with air-cooled dual Xeon 6 chips on a sled. The company pegs this as the easy transition path into AI factory hardware. The 2U unit, with its 100 percent liquid cooling, is tailored for maximum PUE and compute density. It also uses a cable-free board-to-board design to keep its footprint low.
The kit will be speedy, too, with NVIDIA HGX Rubin offering 800Gbit of integrated bandwidth per GPU.

ASUS is promoting the serviceability of these units through their use of tool list CPU and GPU sleds. It claims up to a 50 percent time saving on maintenance operations for these units, meaning less downtime per service and ultimately a lower total cost of ownership.
Delivered fast for NVIDIA HGX Rubin

ASUS is structuring its hardware proposition around speedy delivery so that customers can get hardware up and running to support their AI initiatives. That speed comes from validation carried out before delivery with the help of a pre-validated rack reference architecture.
NVIDIA MGX Server for flexible builds

In keeping with its focus on multiple designs for the right AI workload, ASUS also supports NVIDIA's modular MGX Blueprint for server builds. The selling point here is flexibility with a mixture of GPUs, CPUs, and networking options for enterprise inference, agents, and visual computing. This is the modular route for workloads that don't need the power of an 8-GPU HGX baseboard, and it covers a large gamut of enterprise inference and agentic use cases.

ASUS showcased MGX servers including the 6U XA P8A-E14AXL with its eight liquid-cooled NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs. A 2U sibling, the XA P4N-E2, sports NVIDIA Vera processors for agentic work.
Solutions for the edge and developers

The ASUS booth also featured the ExpertCenter Pro ET900N G3, powered by the GB300 Grace Blackwell Superchip developer desktop with 748GB of coherent memory, and the Ascent GX10 based on NVIDIA DGX Spark for agentic work. Also on show were the ProArt GR1X Mini PC and ProArt P16 and P14 laptop - the first laptops powered by NVIDIA RTX Spark - aimed at both developers and creators.

For edge installations, it showed the PE3000N, its rugged NVIDIA Jetson T5000-based edge-AI computer aimed at use cases including industrial environments. Announced a year ago, this delivers up to 2,070 FP4 TFLOPS of peak AI performance with 128GB of memory. Targeted at industrial AI environments was the PE6000G, a workstation-grade AI and simulation platform.
Rehearsing the AI factory in a digital twin

Equipment only supports an AI factory when there is power to run it. ASUS has been taking steps with NVIDIA as a partner here, adopting its DSX AI Factory platform with digital twin system for laying out hardware and power in AI factory environments. DSX supports equipment using the NVIDIA Vera Rubin processor line, which supports dry coolers and a lower PUE with a 45 degree centigrade warm water inlet.

ASUS configured racks become simulation-ready assets inside DSX, adopting its OpenUSD shared file format. That covers engineering data alongside the geometry for measuring real power draw and cooling requirements.

ASUS wanted to target cooling as part of the original design plan for the AI Factory, not as a facility afterthought. So, the DSX partnership allows implementation teams to model water temperature, flow, pressure, CDU placement, and piping within the digital twin model. They translate information from the planning resources that go around this, such as the NVIDIA Omniverse DSX Blueprint framework, using the ASUS Infrastructure Deployment Center.
Faster to build, easier to run

The digital twin system isn't just for design and setup. It's supposed to keep working after go-live so that AI factory operators can simulate changes before touching hardware. The ASUS Control Center monitors the infrastructure while DSX exchange links IT and operational technology data. Operators can validate changes in the simulation before flipping the switch to go live.

ASUS' goal here is clear: to assist enterprise customers as they tackle in-house AI opportunities while acknowledging that the performance profile and physical locations of their workloads will vary. As companies continue to evolve their understanding of AI and where it fits within the organization, they will need to be agile in how they plan and nurture their infrastructure from the datacenter out to the edge, and to the developer's desk.
The Berlin announcements tie it together in a neat package for organizations that need help with their agentic aspirations.

articles.headline: Donald Trump would like to change the subject
keyFacts: Democrats won commanding majorities in the House and Senate during Tuesday's midterm elections, breaking unified Republican control.
President Donald Trump responded to the historic defeat with subdued public remarks, focusing instead on a White House ballroom project.
Trump adviser statements reported by CNN indicate he likely will not challenge the election results because the Democratic victories were too large.
body: President Donald Trump speaks at the site of the White House ballroom on November 4, 2026. | Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
This story appeared in The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life. Subscribe here .
Welcome to The Logoff: President Donald Trump’s midterms response is a shrug.

What happened? By now, you certainly know: Democrats won overwhelmingly in Tuesday’s midterm elections, and they won everywhere. The party will head into 2027 with commanding majorities in the House and the Senate, breaking two years of unified Republican control in Washington, DC.

The results are a sweeping repudiation of Trump, the Republican Party, and the first two years of his second administration. But you wouldn’t know it from the president’s only public appearance on Wednesday, which focused on his beloved East Wing ballroom .

How is Trump responding? To a surprising extent, he’s not. He blamed the loss on Republican candidates and his absence from the ballot in social media posts Tuesday night, but his public comments have been subdued, with none of the claims of election fraud that have become his hallmark.

One Trump adviser, according to CNN , said that Trump likely would not attempt to challenge the results (Alaska notwithstanding, potentially) because the scale of the Democratic victories was “too big to rig.”

On Wednesday, Trump gave remarks from inside the partially completed ballroom — dwelling on its size, the kitchen setup, and his choice of marble for the flooring — and signed his name on a steel beam. His only comments on the midterms came in response to questions from the press, including about the Iran war, which Vice President JD Vance has blamed for the GOP loss.
“I think it’s largely true,” Trump said, “but at the same time, if I had to do it again, I’d have to do it again.”

What’s the big picture? It’s pretty likely that we’ll see a few different versions of Trump’s response in the coming days, not to mention when Democrats actually take power in January — my colleague Astead Herndon described it on Wednesday as Trump’s “stages of grief.”
Whatever the next two years look like, though, his tepid response to a historic defeat makes one thing clear: Donald Trump’s time at the center of American politics is slipping away.
And with that, it’s time to log off…

Another result of Tuesday’s elections: More than a million low-income Texans could soon have access to healthcare , after Democratic victories in the state opened up the possibility of Medicaid expansion. You can read all about it from my colleague Dylan Scott here with a gift link.
Or, if you’re ready to be done with politics content for today, here’s a picture of a baby muskox.
Have a great evening, and we’ll see you tomorrow!

articles.headline: Como make Champions League era history with incredible nine-goal mauling
keyFacts: Como defeated Lens 9-1 to equal the biggest win in the Champions League era.
Anastasios Douvikas scored a hat-trick for Como while seven different players found the net.
The victory moved Como to fourth place in the league phase table with nine points.
body: Como enjoyed an historic night as they thumped Lens 9-1 to equal the biggest win of the Champions League era.
Cesc Fabregas ‘ side continued their stunning debut campaign in Europe’s premier competition by producing their most impressive display yet with a record-breaking away victory.
Como have been the Champions League surprise package this term, especially after thumping Lens Getty
After thrashing Manchester United 4-1 last time out, Como reached a new level against Lens as seven different players found the net.
Anastasios Douvikas led the way with a hat-trick for the Italian side, grabbing a brace in the first half before Nico Paz struck to put the visitors 3-0 up at the interval.
And the best was yet to come in the second half, with Como grabbing six more goals to write their name into the record books.
Douvikos completed his treble, while Lucas Da Cunha, Marc-Oliver Kempf, Mattia Liberali, Martin Baturina and Matteo Papaccioli all struck for Fabregas’ side.
Ruben Aguilar found the net on 65 minutes to score the smallest of consolation goals for Lens, as the game finished 9-1.
Records galore for superb Como
The result saw Como climb to fourth in the Champions League league phase table with their third win in four games, and record multiple records in the process.
The eight-goal margin equalled the biggest victory in Champions League history since it rebranded under this name in 1992.
Liverpool and Real Madrid have both previously won by this scoreline – doing so against Besiktas and Malmo respectively in 2007 and 2015.
Meanwhile, Como also became only the second team after Bayern Munich to score nine goals in a game.
The German giants famously thrashed Dinamo Zagreb 9-2 in the 2024/25 season – with Harry Kane netting four goals on the night .
Fabregas’ reputation continues to grow after Lens’ historic 9-1 win in the Champions League Getty
Douvikas was the star of the show as he grabbed a hat-trick in the rout Getty
And there was further history for Como by recording their eye-watering scoreline away from home.
They are now the first team of the Champions League era to score nine goals in an away match, and the first to do so in 45 years in the European Cup altogether.
Feyenoord were the last side to do so, when they won 9-0 at Olympiakos Nicosia in September 1971.
And while Como found themselves in the record books for the right reasons, Lens instead made unwanted history.
Their crushing defeat was a record Champions League loss for a French club, and their third consecutive loss in this season’s competition.
Lens now sit a lowly 33rd out of 36 in the overall Champions League standings after four games with three points.
Highly-rated Argentine youngster Paz impressed against Lens Getty
Meanwhile, Como are flying high in fourth on nine points, three points behind Paris Saint-Germain and Real Madrid, and one point behind Arsenal .
The Serie A side, who finished fourth in Serie A last season to qualify for the Champions League for the first time, had already beaten both RB Leipzig and Man United 4-1 at home in this campaign.

articles.headline: Sony Promises Some Players Up To $400 To Trade In Their Used PS5s
keyFacts: Sony sent alerts to some PS5 owners offering up to $400 to trade in their used consoles through Back Market.
The trade-in promotion aims to boost hardware inventory as console makers face dwindling supplies ahead of major game releases.
Xbox is using a similar trade-in strategy by offering inactive players up to $375 for their consoles.
body: In normal times, console makers regularly cut the price of their latest hardware in order to boost sales and increase revenue. As the cost of manufacturing a new console comes down, they’d drop the price to reach consumers who might not have previously considered buying one. They certainly weren’t begging existing players to trade in their machines for big refunds.

But that’s basically what Sony was doing in a recent alert that went out to some current PS5 owners. The alert, titled “Trade in your PS5 console for up to $400,” went out on November 2, and a screenshot of it was shared on the gaming forum ResetEra. “Enjoy simple, hassle-free service if you choose to trade in with Back Market,” the announcement read. “If you’re ready to sell your console, you could soon receive a cash payment into your nominated bank account. Find out how much you could get today.”

The deal seemed surprisingly good, even if getting the full $400 did require sending in two DualSense controllers rather than just one. That’s the price the all-digital PS5 launched at in 2020. Instead of going down, the official price tag has ratcheted up to $600. Used PS5s sold on places like eBay are currently going for around $435. Rarely do you see third-party refurbishment offers get anywhere close to lone seller price.

Xbox has been similarly aggressive, pinging players who haven’t turned on their Xbox Series X/S consoles in a while with offers of up to $375 to trade them in. That’s one strategy for getting around dwindling supplies and getting existing hardware into the hands of people who will actually buy and play new games on it. In the lead-up to Grand Theft Auto 6, both companies have every incentive to bolster inventory and limit the number of consoles sitting out there in the wild that are just collecting dust.

And if you happen to be in the market to get rid of your PS5 Pro, well, you’re in luck. They’ve become so hard to get that GameStop is currently selling used ones for up to $1,400. Don’t trade it in to the meme stock store chain though, obviously. You can get a lot more if you just sell it direct.

articles.headline: Erika Kirk channels Charlie with blunt message to conservatives after GOP midterm losses
